$37 an Hour Is How Much a Year? $76,960 Full-Time, Before Taxes

Direct Answer$37 an hour is $76,960 a year full-time ($1,480 a week, $6,413 a month). See pay by period, overtime, unpaid weeks, and $62,971 take-home after federal tax.

Quick Answer

$37 an hour pays $76,960 a year on a full-time schedule: 40 hours a week, 52 weeks, 2,080 hours. That is $1,480 a week, $2,960 every two weeks, and $6,413 a month on average, before taxes. A single filer taking the 2026 standard deduction keeps $62,971.36 after federal income tax and FICA alone, which is $5,247.61 a month, 81.8% of gross pay, or $30.27 kept from every hour worked. Two quirks make this rate more interesting than it looks. First, 2026 starts and ends on a Thursday, so a Thursday biweekly payday lands 27 times this year, and the extra check brings the year to $79,920 gross and $65,053.72 kept. Second, only $10,460 of the year’s income is taxed at 22%, and a 401(k) contribution of exactly that size deletes the 22% slice altogether and saves $2,301.20 of federal tax. On top of that, a $1 raise keeps $1,463.28, and 55 overtime hours close the gap to an $80,000 salary.

The 27-Paycheck Year: When the Calendar Hands You an Extra Check

Most years, a biweekly worker gets 26 paychecks. 2026 is one of the rare years with 27. The year starts on a Thursday and ends on a Thursday, so a biweekly payday that falls on Thursday lands 27 times, from January 1 to December 31. If your payday is a Thursday, your 2026 has one more check in it than the $76,960 headline assumes. Here is what that extra check is worth at $37 an hour:

26 checks (normal year)27 checks (2026, Thursday payday)
Gross pay$76,960.00$79,920.00
Federal income tax$8,101.20$8,752.40
FICA$5,887.44$6,113.88
Take-home$62,971.36$65,053.72
Take-home per month on average$5,247.61$5,421.14

The extra check is real money, not a rounding trick. It adds $2,960.00 of gross and $2,082.36 of take-home, because the whole check lands in the 22% bracket and keeps 70.35 cents of every dollar after federal tax and FICA. It also puts the year within touching distance of an $80,000 salary: $80 of gross short, and $56.28 of take-home short ($65,053.72 against $65,110.00). Two overtime hours all year, $111.00 of gross, push it past the salary on both counts, to $80,031.00 gross and $65,131.81 kept. One honest caveat: your per-check withholding is figured as if the year had 26 checks, so the tax on the 27th check settles when you file, not when you are paid. Our paychecks-per-year guide maps which weekdays get 27 checks in 2026, and the biweekly-versus-semimonthly comparison shows why the two schedules feel different across a year.

The Bracket-Eraser: The Contribution That Deletes the 22% Slice

Only $10,460 of a $37-an-hour year is taxed at 22%. That small slice has a practical use: it is exactly the size of the pre-tax 401(k) contribution that wipes the 22% bracket off your year. Contribute $10,460 before tax and your taxable income falls to $50,400.00, the exact top of the 12% bracket. Here is the ladder, from no contribution to the full eraser:

401(k) contributionTaxable incomeFederal taxFederal tax savedTake-home after contribution22% slice left
$0.00$60,860.00$8,101.20$0.00$62,971.36$10,460.00
5% ($3,848.00)$57,012.00$7,254.64$846.56$59,969.92$6,612.00
10% ($7,696.00)$53,164.00$6,408.08$1,693.12$56,968.48$2,764.00
13.6% ($10,460.00)$50,400.00$5,800.00$2,301.20$54,812.56$0.00

The eraser contribution is $402.31 a biweekly check, and it saves $2,301.20 of federal tax, because every dollar contributed out of the 22% slice saves 22 cents. Two things do not change. FICA stays at $5,887.44 in every row, because 401(k) contributions are still taxed for Social Security and Medicare. And the money is not gone: the take-home column falls because $10,460 moved into the retirement account instead of the paycheck, so the honest comparison is $54,812.56 of take-home plus $10,460 saved, against $62,971.36 of take-home and nothing saved. Past $10,460, each extra dollar contributed saves only 12 cents, so the eraser is also the point where the tax saving per dollar drops. Our 401(k)-paycheck guide prices the same trade at any contribution rate.

The Short Answer: $76,960 a Year

One multiplication gets the gross, three subtractions get the take-home. All six steps below use the same $37.00 rate as every other section in this guide:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Annual gross$37.00 × 40 hours × 52 weeks$76,960.00
Step 2 — Federal income taxTaxable $60,860.00: $1,240.00 + $4,560.00 + $2,301.20$8,101.20
Step 3 — FICA7.65% × $76,960.00 (SS $4,771.52 + Medicare $1,115.92)$5,887.44
Step 4 — Take-home$76,960.00 − $8,101.20 − $5,887.44$62,971.36
Step 5 — Per month$62,971.36 ÷ 12$5,247.61
Step 6 — Per biweekly check$62,971.36 ÷ 26$2,421.98

That take-home is a federal-only sketch: single filer, $16,100 standard deduction, no state tax, no 401(k) or health premium, and 40 paid hours in all 52 weeks. The $2,301.20 in Step 2 is the number most guides never show. Just $10,460 of the $60,860.00 of taxable income sits in the 22% bracket, and taxing the whole amount at 22% would overstate the federal bill by $5,288.00. The rest of this guide runs the same rate through other schedules, overtime, and unpaid weeks, so you can find the row that looks like your year.

$37 an Hour After Taxes (Federal Only)

Here is the bracket-by-bracket working for a single filer in 2026 with the $16,100 standard deduction. Each step is shown so you can line it up against your own pay stub:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Gross pay$37.00 × 2,080 hours$76,960.00
Step 2 — Standard deductionSingle filer, 2026− $16,100.00
Step 3 — Taxable income$76,960.00 − $16,100.00$60,860.00
Step 4 — 10% bracket10% × $12,400.00$1,240.00
Step 5 — 12% bracket12% × $38,000.00$4,560.00
Step 6 — 22% bracket22% × $10,460.00$2,301.20
Step 7 — Federal income tax$1,240.00 + $4,560.00 + $2,301.20$8,101.20
Step 8 — Social Security6.2% × $76,960.00$4,771.52
Step 9 — Medicare1.45% × $76,960.00$1,115.92
Step 10 — Take-home$76,960.00 − $8,101.20 − $5,887.44$62,971.36

Three rates describe the result, and they are easy to mix up. You keep 81.8% of gross pay. The effective federal income-tax rate is 10.5% ($8,101.20 ÷ $76,960.00). The marginal rate is 22%, but it touches only $10,460.00 of income, which is why the effective rate stays near 10%. Per hour worked, $30.27 of the $37.00 reaches you. Watch one label: several top-ranking pages call 18.2% the “effective federal rate” at this wage, but 18.2% is federal income tax plus FICA combined ($13,988.64 ÷ $76,960.00). The federal income-tax rate on its own is 10.5%. State tax is the missing piece in this sketch: with no state income tax the $62,971.36 stands, and in a state that taxes wages it drops. Our paycheck-tax guide shows how to read the state line on a stub, and the FICA guide splits the 7.65% into its two parts and the $184,500 wage base. The paycheck calculator runs the same federal method on any rate and schedule, including a 401(k) contribution, which lowers Step 3 but leaves Steps 8 and 9 alone.

What Overtime Adds

Federal law pays non-exempt hourly workers at least time and a half past 40 hours in a workweek. At $37.00 an hour the overtime rate is $55.50. Five extra hours a week is the pattern most people actually work, so here it is priced end to end:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — Overtime rate$37.00 × 1.5$55.50 an hour
Step 2 — Straight-time year40 hours × 52 weeks × $37.00$76,960.00
Step 3 — Overtime pay5 hours × 52 weeks × $55.50$14,430.00
Step 4 — Gross with overtime$76,960.00 + $14,430.00$91,390.00
Step 5 — Take-home with overtimeFederal $11,275.80 + FICA $6,991.34 off $91,390.00$73,122.86

The premium is the part worth separating. Of the $14,430.00, $9,620.00 is straight-time pay those hours would have earned at $37.00 anyway (5 × 52 × $37.00). Only $4,810.00 is the extra half-rate (5 × 52 × $18.50). Take-home rises by $10,151.50, from $62,971.36 to $73,122.86, because the overtime year pushes $24,890.00 of taxable income into the 22% bracket. Ten overtime hours a week doubles the pattern: $105,820.00 gross, $83,274.37 kept. Two warnings. Overtime is counted per workweek, not per pay period, so a 45-hour week beside a 35-hour week still pays 5 overtime hours; our timesheet guide prices that case in dollars. And five states add a daily overtime threshold on top of the weekly one, which the daily-overtime guide maps state by state. The double-time guide covers the 2× multiplier, and the overtime calculator prices any pattern of hours you enter.

What Unpaid Weeks Cost

The $76,960.00 headline assumes 52 paid weeks. Time off without pay, a seasonal gap, or a slow month comes straight off the year, and because the lost weeks are full-rate weeks, the take-home cost runs ahead of what the gross cost suggests:

Paid weeksHours paidAnnual grossFederal-only take-homeTake-home lost
52 (no unpaid time)2,080$76,960.00$62,971.36—
50 (2 unpaid weeks)2,000$74,000.00$60,889.00$2,082.36
48 (4 unpaid weeks)1,920$71,040.00$58,806.64$4,164.72

Two unpaid weeks cost $2,960.00 of gross and $2,082.36 of take-home. That is more than the whole $37-to-$38 raise is worth ($1,463.28, priced in the raise section below), which is the honest yardstick for weighing a job with unpaid gaps against one with paid time off. Four unpaid weeks cost $5,920.00 of gross and $4,164.72 of take-home, yet the year still beats a $60,000 salary by $11,040.00 gross and $8,416.64 kept. The comparison flips on paid weeks, not on the rate: with two unpaid weeks the $37 job grosses $74,000.00 and trails a $75,000 salary by $1,000.00, while with all 52 weeks paid it beats the same salary by $1,960.00. Our $36-an-hour guide and $35-an-hour guide price the same unpaid-week steps, so the three read as one ladder.

Why Every $1 Raise Keeps the Same $1,463.28

Your taxable income is $60,860.00 and the 12% bracket ends at $50,400.00, so $10,460.00 of the year is taxed at 22% (costing $2,301.20) and the other $50,400.00 is taxed at 10% and 12%. That split is why the effective federal rate is 10.5% while the marginal rate is 22%. It also sets the value of your next raise:

RaiseGross addedTake-home addedWhy
$35 → $36 an hour$2,080.00$1,463.28The whole raise is taxed at 22% + 7.65% FICA
$36 → $37 an hour$2,080.00$1,463.28Same again — the 22% bracket runs to $105,700 taxable
$37 → $38 an hour$2,080.00$1,463.28Same again — every $1 raise keeps $1,463.28 from here on

Every $1 raise from $32 an hour upward keeps exactly $1,463.28: $2,080.00 minus 22% federal tax ($457.60) minus 7.65% FICA ($159.12). The flat rate holds until taxable income passes $105,700.00, which takes a gross of $121,800.00, about $58.56 an hour. The last raise that kept more was $31 to $32 ($1,665.28), because part of it still sat in the 12% bracket. The expensive version of this mistake is the flat-rate shortcut: taxing all $60,860.00 at 22% gives $13,389.20 of federal tax, $5,288.00 more than the real $8,101.20, and it is how one top-ranking page lands on $57,720 of take-home with a flat 25% claim, $5,251.36 below the real figure. Put to work: eight paid days off at $37.00 are worth $2,368.00 gross and about $1,665.89 kept, a little more than a $1 raise, and they push nothing into a higher bracket. The $36-an-hour guide and $35-an-hour guide carry the same ladder, so the $1,463.28 ties out across all three pages.

The $80,000 Salary Test: 55 Overtime Hours Close It

An $80,000 salary leads $37 an hour by $3,040.00 of gross and $2,138.64 of take-home. It is the nearest salary above this rate, and overtime alone closes it:

StepMathResult
Step 1 — The gap$80,000.00 − $76,960.00$3,040.00
Step 2 — Overtime hours needed$3,040.00 ÷ $55.5054.77 hours a year
Step 3 — Per week54.77 ÷ 52 weeks1.05 hours a week
Step 4 — The week that does it40.00 + 1.05 hours a week41.05-hour week
Step 5 — Take-home at $80,000Federal $8,770.00 + FICA $6,120.00 off $80,000.00$65,110.00

Rounded up: 55 overtime hours a year, a little over one a week, put the $37 year past an $80,000 salary, at $80,012.50 gross and $65,118.79 kept. The catch is that the hours have to be real and paid; overtime you hope for is not overtime you get, and an exempt salaried worker earns nothing extra for the same late finishes, which is the trade the hourly job wins. The next rung takes longer but is still in reach: an $85,000 salary leads by $8,040.00 gross and $5,656.14 kept, and 145 overtime hours a year (2.79 a week, a 42.79-hour week) close it at $85,007.50 gross and $68,632.78 kept. Our $32-an-hour guide closes its $70,000 gap with 72 overtime hours, and the 5%-raise guide prices the raise route to the same targets. A raise to $38.85 an hour lands at $80,808.00, $808.00 past $80,000.

Six figures needs a $48.08-an-hour rate at 40 hours a week, which is $11.08 an hour above $37.00. On overtime alone the gross gap is $23,040.00, and each overtime hour pays $55.50:

Step 2 — Overtime hours needed$23,040.00 ÷ $55.50415.14 hours a year

In whole hours: 8 overtime hours a week, every week, make a $100,048.00 year with $79,213.77 kept, $16,242.41 more than the straight-time year. But that is a 48-hour week with no slow weeks and no cap on overtime, a different job from the occasional late finish, and it only works because of the premium: those 416 hours at straight time would pay $15,392.00, not $23,088.00. The cheaper route to six figures is the raise, not the hours. Each $1 of rate keeps $1,463.28, so the $11.08 climb to $48.08 is worth $16,213.14 of take-home with no extra hours at all. If six figures is the goal, the raise section of our 5%-raise guide is the better next read. The $50-an-hour guide crosses $100,000 on straight time alone, at $104,000.00 gross.

Is $37 an Hour a Good Wage?

Measured against national benchmarks, $37 is comfortably good pay. The median hourly wage is about $24.51, or $50,980.80 a year full-time, so $37 sits $12.49 an hour (51.0%) above the median, worth $25,979.20 a year more than the median worker’s gross. It is 5.10 times the $7.25 federal minimum wage, and 99.0% of average hourly earnings for private-sector workers (about $37.38 an hour in early 2026): right at the average, well above the middle.

The monthly test is the one that decides how the wage feels. Take-home of $5,247.61 a month puts the common 30% rent budget at $1,574.28, workable in most mid-size cities and tight in the most expensive ones. Two cautions before you judge an offer by that figure. It assumes 40 paid hours in all 52 weeks with no state tax, and no 401(k) or health premium taken out first. A 5% 401(k) contribution is $3,848.00 a year and costs $3,001.44 of take-home after the $846.56 federal saving ($250.12 a month, $115.44 a biweekly check), as the 401(k)-paycheck guide prices in dollars. The $30-an-hour guide and $36-an-hour guide run the same benchmarks at their rates, so you can see where $37 sits on the whole ladder.

Check Your Own Stub in Three Lines

You do not need a calculator to sanity-check a $37 paycheck. Three lines on the stub tell you whether the year in this guide matches yours:

  1. Gross line: hours worked × $37.00. A standard biweekly check shows $2,960.00. If yours shows less, your paid hours or weeks differ from the 2,080-hour year, and the schedules and unpaid-weeks tables above price the difference.
  2. Federal line: a full-year single filer with no other adjustments owes $8,101.20 on $76,960.00 of gross, about $311.58 a biweekly check ($8,101.20 ÷ 26). Withholding will not match to the cent, because it annualizes each check, but it should land close. A big gap usually means a W-4 setting or a pre-tax deduction is at work.
  3. FICA line: 7.65% of gross, $226.44 on a $2,960.00 check ($183.52 Social Security + $42.92 Medicare). This one has no settings and no brackets below the wage base, so it should match exactly.

If a line disagrees, the usual causes are paid weeks under 52, a 401(k) or health premium coming out before tax, or state tax on its own line. The calculators below run the same method on your real hours and weeks:

Read This Before You Quote the Number

It is federal only. Every take-home figure here is a single filer taking the $16,100 standard deduction under 2026 federal rules. State and local taxes are not in any number on this page, so take-home is lower in most states. A 5% state income tax would take about $3,848.00 a year off this gross.

It assumes 52 paid weeks. The $76,960.00 headline needs 40 paid hours in every week of the year. Two unpaid weeks cut take-home by $2,082.36 and four by $4,164.72, and the schedules table prices shorter weeks the same way.

Overtime is assumed, not promised. The overtime sections need the hours to exist and be paid at time and a half. Exempt workers earn no premium, and some employers cap overtime. Five overtime hours a week account for $10,151.50 of the overtime year’s take-home, so if the hours are not there, that money is not either.

Filing status changes the answer. The 22% slice of $10,460.00 and every take-home figure depend on the single-filer brackets and the $16,100 deduction. Filing jointly on the same $76,960.00 keeps $66,197.36, which is $3,226.00 more. A 401(k) contribution, a second income, or a different deduction moves the bracket line too. Benefits are priced separately throughout: health premiums, employer matches, and paid time off can flip the $75,000 and $80,000 comparisons. Per-check figures are rounded to the cent, so a rounded monthly figure times 12 can differ from the annual figure by a few cents. And none of this is tax or legal advice: it is a 2026 federal estimate worked the same way as the rest of this site, and your payroll calendar, withholding elections, and benefit deductions will move your real numbers.

Frequently Asked Questions

The questions readers ask most about $37 an hour, answered with the same numbers as the tables above:

How much is $37 an hour biweekly?

A biweekly check at $37 an hour is $2,960 gross (80 hours × $37). After federal tax and FICA alone, a single filer keeps $2,421.98 a check ($62,971.36 ÷ 26). Semi-monthly is a different check: $3,206.67 gross (24 paychecks) and $2,623.81 kept. The yearly totals match because two months carry three biweekly checks and the other ten carry two. In 2026, a Thursday biweekly payday lands 27 times, which adds a whole extra $2,960 check to the year.

How much is $37 an hour per month?

The exact average is $6,413.33 gross a month ($76,960 ÷ 12), with $5,247.61 kept after federal tax alone for a single filer. Two common shortcuts miss: weekly pay times 4 gives $5,920, which is a short month, and times 4.33 gives $6,408.40. Both assume a different year length than the standard 2,080-hour year used here.

How much is $37 an hour after taxes?

For a single filer in 2026 taking the standard deduction, federal-only take-home is $62,971.36 a year: $76,960 gross, minus $8,101.20 of federal income tax (10% × $12,400 + 12% × $38,000 + 22% × $10,460), minus $5,887.44 of FICA. That is $5,247.61 a month, $2,421.98 biweekly, or $30.27 kept from each hour. State tax, retirement contributions, and health premiums are not in the figure, so a real paycheck comes in lower.

Is $37 an hour good pay?

Nationally, yes. It is 51.0% above the median hourly wage of about $24.51 (which annualizes to $50,980.80, a gap of $25,979.20), 99.0% of average hourly earnings for private-sector workers (about $37.38 an hour in early 2026), and 5.10 times the $7.25 federal minimum wage. How it feels depends on hours, household size, and city: $5,247.61 a month of federal-only take-home puts the 30% rent budget at $1,574.28, comfortable in most mid-size cities and tight in the priciest ones.

How much is $37 an hour part-time?

At 25 hours a week all year, $37 an hour is $48,100 gross and $40,828.35 kept after federal tax alone. At 20 hours it is $38,480 gross and $33,098.68 kept. Part-time keeps a bigger share of gross (86.0% at 20 hours against 81.8% full-time) because less income reaches the 22% bracket. The schedules table lists every step from 20 to 40 hours.

What salary is $37 an hour equal to?

At a standard full-time year, $37 an hour equals a $76,960 salary: $3,040 below an $80,000 salary in gross, and $2,138.64 below it after federal tax alone ($62,971.36 against $65,110.00). Fifty-five overtime hours a year at $55.50 close that gap. Paid weeks can flip it, though: with two unpaid weeks the hourly job falls to $74,000 gross and trails a $75,000 salary by $1,000, so compare on paid weeks, not the headline rate.

Key Takeaways & Action Plan

  • $37 an hour is $76,960 a year full-time: $1,480 a week, $2,960 biweekly, $6,413 a month on average, before taxes.
  • Federal-only take-home is $62,971.36 for a single filer: $5,247.61 a month, $2,421.98 biweekly, $30.27 kept per hour.
  • 2026 is a 27-paycheck year for Thursday biweekly paydays: $79,920.00 gross, $65,053.72 kept, just $56.28 of take-home short of an $80,000 salary.
  • Only $10,460 of income reaches the 22% bracket. A $10,460 pre-tax 401(k) contribution erases that slice and saves $2,301.20 of federal tax.
  • A $1 raise keeps exactly $1,463.28, flat from $32 an hour up to about $58.56 an hour, where the 24% bracket starts.
  • Five overtime hours a week add $14,430 a year ($91,390 total; $73,122.86 take-home), if the hours are real and you are non-exempt.
  • 55 overtime hours a year close the $80,000 gap; eight a week, every week, make a $100,048 year.
  • Two unpaid weeks cost $2,960 gross ($2,082.36 take-home), more than the $37-to-$38 raise is worth. Compare offers on paid weeks and real hours, not the headline rate.

Sources & Method

Gross figures use the standard full-time year of 2,080 hours (40 hours × 52 weeks). Monthly averages divide by 12; biweekly figures use 26 paychecks (27 in the 2026 Thursday-payday case). After-tax figures use 2026 federal rules for a single filer taking the standard deduction: $16,100 deduction, brackets 10% to $12,400, 12% to $50,400, 22% to $105,700 of taxable income (IRS Revenue Procedure 2025-32). FICA is 7.65% (Social Security 6.2% to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare 1.45%). Median wage: Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025 ($24.51 an hour); average hourly earnings about $37.38 an hour in early 2026 (BLS). Competitor note: DollarCalcs matches the $76,960 gross and $62,971 take-home but calls the 18.2% combined federal-plus-FICA rate the effective federal rate (the federal rate alone is 10.5%) and prices no raise, overtime, or unpaid-week cases. Paycheckscalculator.org contradicts itself on one page ($62,971 in one section, a $59,976 typical-state figure in another, a $2,201.01 biweekly net against the correct $2,421.98). FinalRoundAI shows $62,971.36 in its detail section but $62,528 in its own summary. This article is general information, not tax or legal advice.

3 Things to Remember

  1. The headline is $76,960 gross and $62,971.36 kept after federal tax alone: $5,247.61 a month for a single filer.
  2. 2026 hands Thursday-payday workers a 27th check, worth $2,082.36 kept, and a $10,460 401(k) contribution erases the whole 22% slice and saves $2,301.20 of federal tax.
  3. Hours and paid weeks move the year more than the rate does: 30 hours is $57,720, two unpaid weeks cost $2,960, and five overtime hours a week add $14,430.

Methodology & Data Verification

  • Basis: Pay figures are gross unless a section states take-home; tax figures use 2026 federal rules where shown.
  • Method: Full formulas, baselines, and rounding rules are on our calculation methodology page.
  • Coverage: U.S. federal rules; state and local rules vary and are not included.
  • Review: Last updated November 27, 2026.
  • Disclaimer: Estimates for planning only — not tax or legal advice.
